Kubernetes StatefulSets

v3 — stable names, stable DNS, a disk per Pod and ordered operations, explained with one real workload: orders-db, PostgreSQL 16 with one primary and two replicas in jahez-prod on EKS (me-central-1).

apps/v1GA since 1.9EKS 1.33+CKAD
Part I

High Level

What a StatefulSet is, the problem it solves, and how its parts fit together in the Jahez cluster.

1

Foundations

1.1Introduction

In one sentenceA StatefulSet runs Pods that keep their name, their DNS name and their own disk, and it starts, stops and updates them in order.
DefinitionA StatefulSet (apps/v1, kind StatefulSet, short name sts) is a workload object. Its controller runs inside kube-controller-manager on the control plane, so there is nothing to install. It runs a set of Pods from one template, like a Deployment does. The difference is that each Pod keeps a fixed name (orders-db-stateful-set-0, -1, -2), a fixed DNS name through a headless Service, and its own PersistentVolumeClaim. The controller also creates, deletes and updates the Pods in ordinal order. StatefulSets have been GA since Kubernetes 1.9. You work with them through kubectl, Helm, Kustomize or Argo CD, like any other object.
✓ It is
  • a controller built into every cluster
  • the owner of Pods named <name>-0 … <name>-(N-1), recreated under the same name
  • the creator of one PVC per Pod from volumeClaimTemplates
  • ordered by default: start 0→N-1, stop N-1→0, update N-1→0
  • able to update part of the set with partition (a canary)
✕ It is not
  • a database operator: no failover, no replica promotion, no backups
  • a Service: you create the headless Service yourself
  • data replication: PostgreSQL copies the data, not Kubernetes
  • a stable IP: IPs change on every restart; names stay
  • a shared disk: each Pod has its own volume
  • a cleaner: PVCs stay after delete and scale-down unless you change the retention policy

Definitions

Stateless vs stateful application
◆
A stateless app keeps nothing between requests, so any copy can serve any request (order-service). A stateful app keeps data or a role on its own disk, so copies are not interchangeable (orders-db: one primary takes writes, two replicas take reads).
🎯
Why it exists. Kubernetes needs to know whether a lost Pod can be replaced by any new Pod, or must come back as the same member with the same data.
📄
What it looks like
TEXT
# stateless: any Pod, random name
order-service-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp
# stateful: fixed member, fixed data
orders-db-stateful-set-0  ->  data-orders-db-stateful-set-0
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. Deployment for stateless, StatefulSet for stateful.
Beforepod dies → new random name, empty disk
→
Afterpod dies → same name, same disk, same role
📍
Where it lives. Your design decision, before any YAML.
⚠
Watch out. Redis used only as a cache is stateless (Deployment). Redis with persistence or Redis Cluster is stateful.
Ordinal and stable identity
◆
Every Pod gets an ordinal, an index from 0 to replicas-1. The ordinal becomes its name, its hostname, its DNS name and the suffix of its PVC. All four survive restarts and rescheduling.
🎯
Why it exists. Members of a database or Kafka cluster find each other and their own data by name. A random name would break replication.
📄
What it looks like
YAML
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set-1
  labels:
    apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index: "1"
spec:
  hostname: orders-db-stateful-set-1
  subdomain: orders-db-headless-service
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. The controller writes the name, the pod-index label, hostname and subdomain on each Pod it creates.
Beforepod-1 · IP 10.40.45.18 · node in 1b
→
Afterpod-1 · IP 10.40.45.61 · same name, same PVC
📍
Where it lives. On the Pod: metadata.name and labels, written by the controller.
⚠
Watch out. Only the IP changes. Always connect by DNS name, never by IP.
Headless Service
◆
A Service with clusterIP: None. It has no virtual IP. DNS answers with the Pod IPs themselves, and every Pod named by the StatefulSet gets its own A record.
🎯
Why it exists. A normal Service hides which Pod you reach. A primary/replica database needs you to reach exactly pod-0.
📄
What it looks like
YAML
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: orders-db
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. The EndpointSlice controller lists the Pod IPs, and CoreDNS publishes <pod>.<service> records.
Beforenslookup orders-db-headless-service → (no records)
→
Afterorders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service → 10.40.12.34
📍
Where it lives. A Service in the same namespace, named in the StatefulSet's spec.serviceName.
⚠
Watch out. If the names do not match, the Pods still start, but their DNS names never resolve.
volumeClaimTemplates
◆
A PVC template inside the StatefulSet. For each ordinal the controller creates one PVC named <template>-<statefulset>-<ordinal> and mounts it into that Pod only.
🎯
Why it exists. One shared ReadWriteOnce disk cannot be attached to three Pods. Each member needs its own disk that follows it.
📄
What it looks like
YAML
volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 20Gi
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. Before creating pod-N, the controller creates data-orders-db-stateful-set-N if it does not exist, or re-uses it if it does.
Beforereplicas: 3, no PVCs
→
Afterdata-…-0, data-…-1, data-…-2 (20Gi gp3 each)
📍
Where it lives. In the StatefulSet spec. The PVCs it creates are separate objects in jahez-prod.
⚠
Watch out. The template cannot be edited after creation. Resizing means patching each PVC (see 5.4).
podManagementPolicy
◆
The rule for starting and stopping Pods. OrderedReady (default) waits for each Pod to be Running and Ready before the next. Parallel starts and stops them all at once.
🎯
Why it exists. A replica must not start before the primary it copies from. Peer-to-peer systems such as Cassandra do not care.
📄
What it looks like
YAML
podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. Gates every create or delete on the previous ordinal's readiness.
Beforeall 3 Pods Pending at once
→
After0 Ready → 1 created → 1 Ready → 2 created
📍
Where it lives. StatefulSet spec; it cannot be changed later.
⚠
Watch out. It does not affect updates. Rolling updates are always one ordinal at a time, unless maxUnavailable is raised.
updateStrategy and partition
◆
RollingUpdate replaces Pods from the highest ordinal down. partition: N limits the update to ordinals ≥ N. OnDelete changes nothing until you delete a Pod.
🎯
Why it exists. Upgrade replicas first and the primary last. Try a new PostgreSQL image on one replica before the rest.
📄
What it looks like
YAML
updateStrategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    partition: 2
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. Compares each Pod's controller-revision-hash label with the update revision and replaces the Pods that differ.
Before0,1,2 on 16.4
→
Afterpartition 2 → only pod-2 on 16.6
📍
Where it lives. StatefulSet spec.updateStrategy.
⚠
Watch out. If the new Pod never becomes Ready, the rollout stops. You must fix the template and delete the broken Pod (see 6.6).
PVC retention policy
◆
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy decides whether PVCs are deleted when the StatefulSet is deleted (whenDeleted) and when it scales down (whenScaled). Both default to Retain.
🎯
Why it exists. Keeping data by default is safe for databases. Test environments need automatic cleanup.
📄
What it looks like
YAML
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
  whenDeleted: Retain
  whenScaled: Delete
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. With Delete, the controller adds an owner reference to the PVC, and the garbage collector removes it.
Beforescale 3→2: data-…-2 kept
→
AfterwhenScaled Delete: data-…-2 removed
📍
Where it lives. StatefulSet spec. Beta in 1.27, GA in 1.32.
⚠
Watch out. Deleting the PVC does not always delete the disk. The StorageClass reclaimPolicy decides that.
ControllerRevision
◆
An immutable snapshot of the Pod template. Every template change creates a new one. Its name hash appears on each Pod as the controller-revision-hash label.
🎯
Why it exists. The controller must know which Pods run the old template and which run the new one. rollout undo needs old templates to go back to.
📄
What it looks like
YAML
kind: ControllerRevision
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set-6b8d9c7f4d
revision: 1
⚙
What Kubernetes does with it. Stores status.currentRevision and status.updateRevision, and keeps revisionHistoryLimit old revisions.
Beforerevision 1 only
→
Afterset image → revision 2; Pods move from hash …7f4d to …a1c2
📍
Where it lives. Separate objects in jahez-prod, owned by the StatefulSet.
⚠
Watch out. Changing only replicas creates no revision. Only template changes do.

1.2Problems or needs

In one sentenceRunning a primary/replica database with Deployments gives random names, a shared disk that cannot be shared, broken addresses after restarts, and no start or update order.
Step 1 / 6The need: one primary, two replicas, three disks

The orders team needs PostgreSQL for order-service. Every order is a write, and the order-history screen is a heavy read. They want:

  • one primary that takes all writes
  • two replicas that stream the WAL from the primary and serve reads
  • its own disk for each member, in a different zone (me-central-1a/b/c)
  • a fixed address for the primary, so writes and replication always reach it
TEXT
# What each member must know, by hand today
primary   : accepts writes, ships WAL to replicas
replica A : pg_basebackup from <primary address>, then stream
replica B : pg_basebackup from <primary address>, then stream
Step 2 / 6Try a Deployment: three random Pods, three primaries

The first try is the familiar object: a Deployment with replicas: 3. The Pods get random names, and all three run the same entrypoint, so all three call initdb and become primaries. Nobody knows which one is "the" primary.

YAMLorders-db-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-db-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.4
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: orders-db-secret
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: orders-db-pvc
BASH
kubectl apply -f orders-db-deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db
OUTPUTexample output
NAME                                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
orders-db-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp    1/1     Running   0          40s
orders-db-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-9vlm4    0/1     Pending   0          40s
orders-db-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-qq7tz    0/1     Pending   0          40s
Step 3 / 6Share one PVC: two Pods stuck in Pending

All three Pods use claimName: orders-db-pvc. That is one EBS volume, and EBS is ReadWriteOnce: one node, one zone. Only the first Pod mounts it. The other two wait forever, and even if they could mount it, three PostgreSQL servers writing to one data directory would corrupt it.

BASH
kubectl describe pod orders-db-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-9vlm4 -n jahez-prod | tail -4
OUTPUTexample output
Events:
  Type     Reason              From                     Message
  Warning  FailedAttachVolume  attachdetach-controller  Multi-Attach error for volume "pvc-3f1c9a2e…" Volume is already used by pod(s) orders-db-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp
  Warning  FailedScheduling    default-scheduler        0/9 nodes are available: 6 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict.
Step 4 / 6Copy everything per member by hand

To give each member its own disk and its own address, the team copies the manifests three times and edits names in every file: a Deployment with replicas: 1, a PVC and a Service per member. That is 9 files that must stay in sync, and the replica files hard-code the primary's address.

BASH
# make member-1 and member-2 from member-0, then hand-edit names, PVCs and the primary address
for i in 1 2; do
  cp -r member-0 member-$i
  sed -i "s/orders-db-0/orders-db-$i/g" member-$i/*.yaml
done
kubectl apply -f member-0/ -f member-1/ -f member-2/
OUTPUTexample output
deployment.apps/orders-db-0-deployment created
persistentvolumeclaim/orders-db-0-pvc created
service/orders-db-0-service created
… 6 more objects …
service/orders-db-0-service configured   # member-2/service.yaml still said orders-db-0!
Step 5 / 6A Pod restarts: new name, new IP, replication breaks

The node in me-central-1b is drained during an EKS upgrade. The replica Pod comes back with a new random name and a new IP. Any config that pointed at the old IP is now wrong, and a Pod rescheduled into another zone cannot reach its EBS volume at all.

BASH
kubectl drain ip-10-40-45-7.me-central-1.compute.internal --ignore-daemonsets
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db -o wide
kubectl logs orders-db-1-deployment-5c9b7d8f6-k3d8n -n jahez-prod | tail -2
OUTPUTexample output
NAME                                     READY   IP            NODE
orders-db-1-deployment-5c9b7d8f6-k3d8n   0/1     10.40.45.61   ip-10-40-46-9…

FATAL:  could not connect to the primary server: connection to server at "10.40.12.34", port 5432 failed: Connection timed out
Step 6 / 6Start order and updates have no order

Two more problems remain. On a fresh start all members start at once, so the replicas run pg_basebackup before the primary is up and crash-loop. On an image upgrade, a Deployment replaces Pods in no particular order, so the primary can be the first one down, which means a write outage for orders.

BASH
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db -w
kubectl set image deployment/orders-db-0-deployment postgres=ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.6 -n jahez-prod
OUTPUTexample output
orders-db-1-deployment-5c9b7d8f6-k3d8n   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   3   1m
orders-db-2-deployment-6f8d9c7b5-z9p2q   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   3   1m

All of this is life before StatefulSets. → 1.3 Solution shows how each problem disappears.

1.3Solution

In one sentenceA headless Service plus a StatefulSet with a PVC template gives every database member a fixed name, a fixed DNS address and its own disk, and runs them in order.

The solution, step by step

  1. A headless Service (orders-db-headless-service, clusterIP: None) lets DNS name each Pod.
  2. The StatefulSet (orders-db-stateful-set) points at it with serviceName and names its Pods -0, -1, -2.
  3. volumeClaimTemplates creates data-orders-db-stateful-set-N for each Pod. That PVC follows the ordinal forever.
  4. OrderedReady starts pod-0, waits for Ready, then pod-1, then pod-2.
  5. The init container reads its ordinal from the apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index label: 0 becomes the primary, the others clone it by DNS name.
  6. RollingUpdate replaces pod-2, then pod-1, then pod-0, so the primary goes last. partition turns the first step into a canary.
  7. A PodDisruptionBudget keeps at least two members up during node drains.

The real folder

TEXT
k8s/
├── platform/
│   └── gp3-encrypted-storage-class.yaml   # shared, owned by the platform team
├── orders-db/                             # kubectl apply -f k8s/orders-db/
│   ├── orders-db-config-map.yaml          # init-role.sh + 10-replication.sh
│   ├── orders-db-headless-service.yaml    # clusterIP: None → per-Pod DNS
│   ├── orders-db-pdb.yaml                 # maxUnavailable: 1
│   ├── orders-db-read-service.yaml        # ClusterIP for reads
│   ├── orders-db-secret.yaml              # credentials (External Secrets in prod)
│   └── orders-db-stateful-set.yaml        # the StatefulSet
└── order-service/
    └── order-service-config-map.yaml      # connection strings that use the DNS names

One tab per environment

YAMLdev patch (orders-db-stateful-set)
spec:
  replicas: 1
  podManagementPolicy: Parallel
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Delete
    whenScaled: Delete
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3-encrypted-storage-class
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi
✓ ResultOne primary only, 5Gi, PVCs cleaned up automatically when the namespace is torn down. Namespace jahez-dev.
YAMLstaging patch
spec:
  replicas: 2
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 0
✓ ResultPrimary + one replica. Every new PostgreSQL image is tested here with a partition canary first. Namespace jahez-staging.
YAMLprod (the base file)
spec:
  replicas: 3
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain
    whenScaled: Retain
✓ ResultPrimary + two replicas, one per zone, PVCs always kept, PDB maxUnavailable: 1. Namespace jahez-prod.

How each problem from 1.2 disappears

Problem in 1.2What fixes itResult
Random names, nobody knows the primaryserviceName + ordinalsorders-db-stateful-set-0 is always the primary
One shared RWO diskvolumeClaimTemplatesthree PVCs, one per Pod, created in the Pod's zone
Nine hand-copied filesone StatefulSetone template, replicas: 3
New name and IP after restartstable identity + headless DNSsame name, same PVC, DNS follows the new IP
Replicas start before the primaryOrderedReadypod-1 is created only after pod-0 is Ready
Upgrade hits the primary firstRollingUpdate from the top + partitionpod-2 → pod-1 → pod-0, canary first
Drains take members down togetherPodDisruptionBudgetat most one member down by choice

1.4Comparisons

In one sentenceDeployments are for interchangeable Pods, StatefulSets for members with names and disks, operators and managed services for when you also need failover.

Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet

DeploymentStatefulSetDaemonSet
Pod namesrandom: order-service-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqpordinal: orders-db-stateful-set-0<name>-<random>, one per node
After a restartnew name, new IPsame name, same PVC, new IPsame node, new name
Storageshared PVC or none RWO PVC works only with 1 replicaone PVC per Pod from a templateusually hostPath or none
Create orderall at once0 → N-1, each waits for Ready unless Parallelall nodes at once
Delete / scale-down orderanyN-1 → 0per node
Update ordersurge, any orderN-1 → 0, one at a time maxUnavailable, partitionnode by node
DNSone Service VIPper-Pod name through the headless Serviceone Service VIP
Needsnothing extraa headless Service (serviceName)nothing extra
RollbackReplicaSetsControllerRevisionsControllerRevisions
Jahez exampleorder-service, menu-apiorders-db, Kafka, Elasticsearchfluent-bit, node-exporter

StatefulSet vs operator vs managed database

Plain StatefulSetOperator (CloudNativePG)Managed (Amazon RDS / Aurora)
Failovernone: if pod-0 dies, writes stop until it returnsautomatic promotion of a replicaautomatic
Backups / PITRyou script it (CronJob + pg_dump / WAL-G)built in (Barman to S3)built in
Major upgradesmanual, riskyguidedconsole / API
Who runs ityour teamyour team + the operatorAWS
Under the hoodStatefulSetits own Pods + PVCs (not a StatefulSet)not in the cluster
Good forlearning, small or cache-like stores, CKADserious in-cluster PostgreSQLcritical prod data

Stateless or stateful? Real examples

AppKindWhy
order-service (ASP.NET Core)Statelessstate lives in orders-db and Redis
orders-db (PostgreSQL)Statefulprimary writes, replicas read, own data each
MongoDB replica setStatefulmembers discover each other by stable DNS name
Kafka brokersStatefulbroker ID + log partitions on its own disk
Elasticsearch (search)Statefulnode name + shards on its own disk
Redis as a pure cacheStatelesslosing it only costs cache misses: Deployment, no PVC
Redis with AOF / RDB persistenceStatefuldata must come back after a restart v2 called this stateless; that was wrong
Redis ClusterStatefulhash slots belong to a node identity

When to choose something else

  • Use a Deployment when any copy can serve any request, even if it reads a database.
  • Use a StatefulSet when members need a name, their own disk, or a start order.
  • Use an operator (CloudNativePG, Strimzi for Kafka, ECK for Elasticsearch) when you need failover, backups and upgrades in-cluster.
  • Use a managed service when the data is critical and nobody on the team wants to be paged for failover.

Architecture and workflows

2.1Architecture

In one sentenceYou write to the API server, the StatefulSet controller turns one object into ordered Pods and PVCs, and CoreDNS gives each Pod its name.
ComponentWhere it runsWhat it does for orders-db
kubectl / Argo CDyour laptop, CI or the argocd namespacesends the six manifests to the API server
API server + etcdEKS control plane (AWS-managed)validates and stores the StatefulSet, Pods, PVCs
StatefulSet controllerkube-controller-manager (control plane)creates ControllerRevisions, PVCs and Pods in order; runs updates
schedulercontrol planepicks a node per Pod, spreading across zones (topologySpreadConstraints)
EBS CSI controllerkube-systemcreates the gp3 volume in the chosen zone, binds the PV
kubelet + EBS CSI nodeeach worker nodeattaches and mounts the volume, runs init-role then postgres
EndpointSlice controllercontrol planelists Pod IPs behind both Services
CoreDNSkube-systemanswers orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service

StorageClassk8s/platform/gp3-encrypted-storage-class.yaml
In one sentenceThe platform StorageClass: encrypted gp3 volumes, created in the Pod's zone, kept when the PVC is deleted.
YAMLgp3-encrypted-storage-class.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3-encrypted-storage-class
# ① Who creates the disk?
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
# ② What kind of disk?
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
  fsType: ext4
# ③ When and where is it created?
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer# create the EBS volume in the zone the Pod lands in
# ④ What happens at the end?
reclaimPolicy: Retain# deleting a PVC keeps the EBS volume (database data!)
allowVolumeExpansion: true
What each block does
  • ① provisioner the EBS CSI driver.
  • ② parameters gp3, encrypted, ext4.
  • ③ WaitForFirstConsumer waits for the Pod's zone.
  • ④ Retain keeps the disk; allowVolumeExpansion allows resizing.

ConfigMapk8s/orders-db/orders-db-config-map.yaml
In one sentenceTwo scripts: one creates the replication role on the primary, the other decides each Pod's role from its ordinal.
YAMLorders-db-config-map.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: orders-db-config-map
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
data:
  # ① What runs once, on the primary's very first start?
  10-replication.sh: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e
    psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d postgres <<-SQL
      CREATE ROLE ${REPLICATION_USER} WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD '${REPLICATION_PASSWORD}';
    SQL
    echo "host replication ${REPLICATION_USER} 0.0.0.0/0 scram-sha-256" >> "$PGDATA/pg_hba.conf"
  # ② How does each Pod decide its role?
  init-role.sh: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e
    # POD_ORDINAL comes from the apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index label
    if [ "$POD_ORDINAL" = "0" ]; then
      echo "ordinal 0 -> primary: the postgres entrypoint runs initdb itself"
      exit 0
    fi
    if [ -s "$PGDATA/PG_VERSION" ]; then
      echo "ordinal $POD_ORDINAL -> replica data already on the PVC, reuse it"
      exit 0
    fi
    PRIMARY=orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service
    until pg_isready -h "$PRIMARY" -p 5432; do echo "waiting for $PRIMARY"; sleep 2; done
    PGPASSWORD="$REPLICATION_PASSWORD" pg_basebackup -h "$PRIMARY" -U "$REPLICATION_USER" \
      -D "$PGDATA" -R -X stream -P
    echo "ordinal $POD_ORDINAL -> cloned from $PRIMARY, standby.signal written"
What each block does
  • ① 10-replication.sh runs once, when the primary's data directory is empty.
  • ② init-role.sh exits for ordinal 0, and clones the primary with pg_basebackup for the others.
⌘ Commands for this file
kubectl logs orders-db-stateful-set-1 -c init-role -n jahez-prod
see which role pod-1 took

Servicek8s/orders-db/orders-db-headless-service.yaml
In one sentenceThe headless Service that gives every member its own DNS name.
YAMLorders-db-headless-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Which Pods does it give names to?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  # ② What makes it headless?
  clusterIP: None# no virtual IP: DNS returns the Pod IPs themselves
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true# publish a Pod's DNS record before it is Ready (peer discovery)
  # ③ Which ports?
  ports:
    - name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
What each block does
  • ① Which Pods? every Pod with app: orders-db.
  • ② Headless: clusterIP: None; not-ready Pods are published too, so replicas can resolve each other while starting.
  • ③ Port 5432, named postgres to match the container port.

StatefulSetk8s/orders-db/orders-db-stateful-set.yaml
In one sentenceThe StatefulSet: three PostgreSQL members, each with its own 20Gi gp3 PVC, started and updated in order.
YAMLorders-db-stateful-set.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
    team: orders
spec:
  # ① Who am I?
  serviceName: orders-db-headless-service# gives each Pod <pod>.orders-db-headless-service
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db# immutable; must match the template labels
  ordinals:
    start: 0# first Pod is ...-0
  # ② How many, and in what order?
  replicas: 3
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady# 0 Ready -> 1 Ready -> 2; immutable
  minReadySeconds: 10# Ready must last 10s before the Pod counts as available
  # ③ Where is my data?
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data# PVC = data-orders-db-stateful-set-<ordinal>
        labels:
          app: orders-db
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3-encrypted-storage-class
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 20Gi
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain# deleting the StatefulSet keeps the PVCs
    whenScaled: Retain# scaling down keeps the PVCs
  # ④ How do I change it?
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate# or OnDelete
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 0# only ordinals >= partition get the new template
      maxUnavailable: 1# beta in 1.35; one Pod at a time
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10# ControllerRevisions kept for rollback
  # ⑤ What runs in each Pod?
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-db
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999# postgres group owns the EBS filesystem
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orders-db
      initContainers:
        - name: init-role
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.4
          command: ["bash", "/scripts/init-role.sh"]
          env:
            - name: POD_ORDINAL
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.labels['apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index']
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: orders-db-secret
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
            - name: scripts
              mountPath: /scripts
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.4
          args: ["-c", "wal_level=replica", "-c", "max_wal_senders=10", "-c", "hot_standby=on", "-c", "max_connections=300"]
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          env:
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: orders-db-secret
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
            - name: initdb
              mountPath: /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "orders", "-h", "127.0.0.1"]
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "orders", "-h", "127.0.0.1"]
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 1Gi
            limits:
              memory: 2Gi
      volumes:
        - name: scripts
          configMap:
            name: orders-db-config-map
            items:
              - key: init-role.sh
                path: init-role.sh
        - name: initdb
          configMap:
            name: orders-db-config-map
            items:
              - key: 10-replication.sh
                path: 10-replication.sh
What each block does
  • ① Who am I? serviceName links to the headless Service; selector must match the template labels.
  • ② How many, in what order? 3 members, OrderedReady.
  • ③ Where is my data? one data PVC per Pod, kept on delete and scale-down.
  • ④ How do I change it? RollingUpdate from the top, partition: 0.
  • ⑤ What runs? init-role picks primary or replica, then postgres runs with probes.

ConfigMapk8s/order-service/order-service-config-map.yaml
In one sentenceHow the ASP.NET Core order-service reaches the database: writes by the primary's DNS name, reads through the read Service.
YAMLorder-service-config-map.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: order-service-config-map
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-service
data:
  # ① Where do writes go? (always the primary, by stable DNS name)
  ConnectionStrings__OrdersWrite: "Host=orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service;Port=5432;Database=orders;Username=orders"
  # ② Where do reads go? (any Ready member, through the ClusterIP)
  ConnectionStrings__OrdersRead: "Host=orders-db-read-service;Port=5432;Database=orders;Username=orders;Load Balance Hosts=false"
  # ③ Optional: let Npgsql find the primary itself across all members
  ConnectionStrings__OrdersPrimaryAny: "Host=orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service,orders-db-stateful-set-1.orders-db-headless-service,orders-db-stateful-set-2.orders-db-headless-service;Target Session Attributes=primary;Database=orders;Username=orders"
What each block does
  • ① writes always orders-db-stateful-set-0.
  • ② reads the ClusterIP Service.
  • ③ Npgsql multi-host finds whichever member is primary.

2.3Controller order

In one sentenceOne apply goes through nine stages: store, snapshot the template, then for each ordinal in turn create the PVC, the Pod, bind the disk in its zone, and wait for Ready.
0run→1store→2revision→3PVC-0→4pod-0→5bind→6Ready→7next ordinal→8status
Step 1 / 9Stage 0 — run the command

You (or Argo CD) run one command. kubectl reads the folder, parses six YAML documents and sends them to the API server one by one, in file-name order.

① INPUT
CMDkubectl apply -f k8s/orders-db/
DISK · k8s/orders-db/
📄
📄
📄
📄
📄
📄
→
② LOGIC
-f <folder>: every .yaml, .yml and .json file, sorted by name.
→

➜ConfigMap/orders-db-config-mapNEW
➜Service/orders-db-headless-serviceNEW
➜PodDisruptionBudget/orders-db-pdbNEW
➜Service/orders-db-read-serviceNEW
➜Secret/orders-db-secretNEW
➜StatefulSet/orders-db-stateful-setNEW
6 new · 0 changed
📌 RememberA wrong path fails before anything is sent: error: the path "k8s/order-db/" does not exist.
Step 2 / 9Stage 1 — API server validates and stores

The API server checks each object against its schema and admission webhooks, then saves it in etcd. No Pod exists yet.

① INPUT

Step 3 / 9Stage 2 — controller snapshots the template

The StatefulSet controller sees a new StatefulSet. It hashes the Pod template and stores it as a ControllerRevision. This hash later tells old Pods from new ones.

① INPUT

📌 RememberOnly template changes create revisions. kubectl scale never does.
Step 4 / 9Stage 3 — PVC for ordinal 0

Before creating pod-0, the controller makes sure its claim exists. It builds data-orders-db-stateful-set-0 from the template. With WaitForFirstConsumer the PVC stays Pending until a Pod uses it.

① INPUT

→

💾NEW

📌 RememberIf a PVC with that name already exists (from an earlier StatefulSet), it is re-used with its old data.
Step 5 / 9Stage 4 — Pod for ordinal 0

The controller creates pod-0 from the template and adds its identity: name, hostname, subdomain, the pod-index and controller-revision-hash labels, and a volume pointing at its own PVC.

① INPUT

→

🟩NEW
1 new
📌 RememberThe Pod name is the StatefulSet name plus -0. Long StatefulSet names make long hostnames (the limit is 63 characters).
Step 6 / 9Stage 5 — schedule, then create the disk in that zone

The scheduler picks a node in me-central-1a. Only now does the EBS CSI driver create a 20Gi gp3 volume in that zone and bind the PVC. From here on, pod-0 can only run in me-central-1a.

① INPUT

🟩orders-db-stateful-set-0

0 new · 2 changed (PVC Bound, Pod nodeName)
📌 RememberThe PV gets node affinity for its zone. If that zone has no capacity later, pod-0 stays Pending; it cannot move zones.
Step 7 / 9Stage 6 — init-role, postgres, Ready, DNS

kubelet mounts the volume and runs init-role (ordinal 0 → primary, exit). PostgreSQL runs initdb and 10-replication.sh. The readiness probe passes, the EndpointSlice adds 10.40.12.34, and CoreDNS answers for orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service.

① INPUT
ETCD · from stage 5
🟩orders-db-stateful-set-0
NEW · from the ConfigMap
📜init-role.sh
📜10-replication.sh
→
② LOGIC
YAMLorders-db-stateful-set.yaml

  exec:
    command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "orders", "-h", "127.0.0.1"]
→
③ OUTPUT
🟩CHANGED
🔗EndpointSlice (headless)CHANGED
🌐DNS A …-0 → 10.40.12.34NEW
1 new record · 2 changed
📌 RememberWithout a readiness probe, "Running" counts as Ready, and pod-1 would start before PostgreSQL accepts connections.
Step 8 / 9Stage 7 — the OrderedReady gate opens: ordinal 1

pod-0 is Ready (and has been for minReadySeconds), so the controller repeats stages 3–6 for ordinal 1. Its init-role finds no data, waits for the primary by DNS name and runs pg_basebackup.

① INPUT

🟩orders-db-stateful-set-0 · Ready

→

💾NEW
🟦NEW
2 new
📌 RememberIf pod-0 is not Ready, nothing happens for ordinal 1 — not even its PVC. A crash-looping pod-0 blocks the whole set.
Step 9 / 9Stage 8 — ordinal 2 and the final status

The same for ordinal 2 in me-central-1c. The controller writes the status: three replicas, three ready, current revision = update revision.

  updateRevision: orders-db-stateful-set-6b8d9c7f4d
  observedGeneration: 1

Part II

Low Level

Every field, every object, every operation and every command — with orders-db as the running example.

3

The StatefulSet object

3.0How a StatefulSet works

In one sentenceOne object that promises: for every ordinal, one Pod with that name and one PVC with that suffix, created and changed in order.

A StatefulSet is a promise about identity. For each ordinal from 0 to replicas-1 there is exactly one Pod with that name and one PVC with that suffix. The controller keeps that promise forever: it creates what is missing, in order, and never gives a Pod a different name or a different disk. It lives as long as you keep it; its PVCs can outlive it.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Who am I?serviceName · selector · ordinals.startthe name tag and the address book entry
② How many, and in what order?replicas · podManagementPolicy · minReadySecondsthe roll call: 0, then 1, then 2
③ Where is my data?volumeClaimTemplates · persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicyone locker per member, kept after they leave
④ How do I change it?updateStrategy · partition · maxUnavailable · revisionHistoryLimitswap members one by one, from the back
⑤ What runs in each Pod?templatethe uniform every member wears
Written by Kubernetesstatus · ControllerRevision · pod-index labelthe controller's own notes
Familyapps/v1 workload
Scopenamespaced
Short namests
SurvivesPod loss · node loss
Typical usedatabases, Kafka, Elasticsearch
TEXT
StatefulSet orders-db-stateful-set
├── ① Who am I?            serviceName · selector · ordinals.start
├── ② How many / order?    replicas · podManagementPolicy · minReadySeconds
├── ③ Where is my data?    volumeClaimTemplates · persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy
├── ④ How do I change it?  updateStrategy (partition, maxUnavailable) · revisionHistoryLimit
├── ⑤ What runs?           template (labels, initContainers, containers, volumes)
└── Written by Kubernetes  status · ControllerRevisions · Pod labels
YAMLorders-db-stateful-set.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
    team: orders
spec:
  # ① Who am I?
  serviceName: orders-db-headless-service# gives each Pod <pod>.orders-db-headless-service
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db# immutable; must match the template labels
  ordinals:
    start: 0# first Pod is ...-0
  # ② How many, and in what order?
  replicas: 3
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady# 0 Ready -> 1 Ready -> 2; immutable
  minReadySeconds: 10# Ready must last 10s before the Pod counts as available
  # ③ Where is my data?
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data# PVC = data-orders-db-stateful-set-<ordinal>
        labels:
          app: orders-db
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3-encrypted-storage-class
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 20Gi
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain# deleting the StatefulSet keeps the PVCs
    whenScaled: Retain# scaling down keeps the PVCs
  # ④ How do I change it?
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate# or OnDelete
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 0# only ordinals >= partition get the new template
      maxUnavailable: 1# beta in 1.35; one Pod at a time
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10# ControllerRevisions kept for rollback
  # ⑤ What runs in each Pod?
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-db
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999# postgres group owns the EBS filesystem
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orders-db
      initContainers:
        - name: init-role
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.4
          command: ["bash", "/scripts/init-role.sh"]
          env:
            - name: POD_ORDINAL
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.labels['apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index']
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: orders-db-secret
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
            - name: scripts
              mountPath: /scripts
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.4
          args: ["-c", "wal_level=replica", "-c", "max_wal_senders=10", "-c", "hot_standby=on", "-c", "max_connections=300"]
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          env:
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: orders-db-secret
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
            - name: initdb
              mountPath: /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "orders", "-h", "127.0.0.1"]
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "orders", "-h", "127.0.0.1"]
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 1Gi
            limits:
              memory: 2Gi
      volumes:
        - name: scripts
          configMap:
            name: orders-db-config-map
            items:
              - key: init-role.sh
                path: init-role.sh
        - name: initdb
          configMap:
            name: orders-db-config-map
            items:
              - key: 10-replication.sh
                path: 10-replication.sh
Show the supporting objects it needs (Secret, ConfigMap, headless Service)
YAMLorders-db-secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: orders-db-secret
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
type: Opaque
# ① Which credentials does the database need?
stringData:                       # in prod this file is rendered by External Secrets from AWS Secrets Manager
  POSTGRES_USER: orders
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: change-me-orders
  POSTGRES_DB: orders
  REPLICATION_USER: replicator
  REPLICATION_PASSWORD: change-me-replicator
YAMLorders-db-config-map.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: orders-db-config-map
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
data:
  # ① What runs once, on the primary's very first start?
  10-replication.sh: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e
    psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d postgres <<-SQL
      CREATE ROLE ${REPLICATION_USER} WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD '${REPLICATION_PASSWORD}';
    SQL
    echo "host replication ${REPLICATION_USER} 0.0.0.0/0 scram-sha-256" >> "$PGDATA/pg_hba.conf"
  # ② How does each Pod decide its role?
  init-role.sh: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e
    # POD_ORDINAL comes from the apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index label
    if [ "$POD_ORDINAL" = "0" ]; then
      echo "ordinal 0 -> primary: the postgres entrypoint runs initdb itself"
      exit 0
    fi
    if [ -s "$PGDATA/PG_VERSION" ]; then
      echo "ordinal $POD_ORDINAL -> replica data already on the PVC, reuse it"
      exit 0
    fi
    PRIMARY=orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service
    until pg_isready -h "$PRIMARY" -p 5432; do echo "waiting for $PRIMARY"; sleep 2; done
    PGPASSWORD="$REPLICATION_PASSWORD" pg_basebackup -h "$PRIMARY" -U "$REPLICATION_USER" \
      -D "$PGDATA" -R -X stream -P
    echo "ordinal $POD_ORDINAL -> cloned from $PRIMARY, standby.signal written"
YAMLorders-db-headless-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Which Pods does it give names to?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  # ② What makes it headless?
  clusterIP: None# no virtual IP: DNS returns the Pod IPs themselves
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true# publish a Pod's DNS record before it is Ready (peer discovery)
  # ③ Which ports?
  ports:
    - name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres

🌳 Every property — tap to open
① Who am I?groupidentity: the name of every Pod and the Service that publishes it
serviceNamestringrequiredname of the headless Service that gives each Pod a DNS name

Copied into every Pod as spec.subdomain. Together with the Pod's hostname it forms <pod>.<serviceName>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local. Treat it as required: without it Pods get no per-Pod DNS.

⚠ Immutable. The Service is not created for you; a typo means names that never resolve.
Deep dive →
selectorobjectrequiredwhich Pods belong to this StatefulSet

A label selector. It must match template.metadata.labels, or the API server rejects the object.

⚠ Immutable. Changing it means deleting the StatefulSet with --cascade=orphan and recreating it.
•matchLabelsobjectapp: orders-db
•matchExpressionslistset-based rules (In, NotIn, Exists)
ordinalsobjectwhere numbering starts
startintfirst ordinal; default 0

Pods are named start … start+replicas-1. Used to move members between clusters (e.g. cluster A runs 0–2, cluster B takes 3–5). GA in 1.31.

Default 0
② How many, and in what order?groupcount and the start/stop policy
replicasintnumber of members

Desired count. kubectl scale changes only this field. Changing it never creates a ControllerRevision.

Default 1
Deep dive →
podManagementPolicystringordered or parallel start/stop
ValueMeaning
OrderedReadycreate 0→N-1, each after the previous is Running+Ready; delete N-1→0
Parallelcreate and delete all at once; updates are still ordered
Default OrderedReady
⚠ Immutable after creation.
Deep dive →
minReadySecondsinthow long Ready must last before a Pod counts as available

Also delays the next ordinal in OrderedReady and the next step of a rolling update.

Default 0
③ Where is my data?groupone PVC per Pod and what happens to it
volumeClaimTemplateslistPVC templates; one PVC per template per Pod

Each item is a PVC spec. The PVC is named <metadata.name>-<statefulset>-<ordinal> and appears as a volume with the template name in every Pod.

⚠ Immutable after creation (except via delete-orphan-recreate).
Deep dive →
•metadata.namestringrequiredvolume name and PVC prefix (data)
spec.accessModeslistReadWriteOnce for EBS
ValueMeaning
ReadWriteOnceone node at a time (EBS)
ReadWriteOncePodone Pod at a time
ReadWriteManymany nodes (EFS); rare for databases
spec.storageClassNamestringgp3-encrypted-storage-class
Deep dive →
spec.resources.requests.storagequantitysize, e.g. 20Gi
⚠ The template cannot be edited later. Resize by patching each PVC.
Deep dive →
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicyobjectdelete PVCs on StatefulSet delete or scale-down?
Deep dive →
whenDeletedstringwhen the StatefulSet is deleted
ValueMeaning
Retainkeep the PVCs (default)
Deletedelete them
whenScaledstringwhen replicas goes down
ValueMeaning
Retainkeep the PVCs (default)
Deletedelete PVCs of removed ordinals
④ How do I change it?groupupdate strategy and history
updateStrategyobjecthow template changes reach the Pods
typestringRollingUpdate or OnDelete
ValueMeaning
RollingUpdatereplace Pods automatically, highest ordinal first
OnDeletereplace a Pod only when you delete it
Default RollingUpdate
Deep dive →
rollingUpdate.partitionintupdate only ordinals ≥ partition
Default 0
Deep dive →
rollingUpdate.maxUnavailableint|%Pods that may be down at once during an update

Beta in 1.35 (feature gate MaxUnavailableStatefulSet, alpha 1.24–1.34). Ignored with OnDelete. With OrderedReady, Pods are still taken in order.

Default 1
revisionHistoryLimitintold ControllerRevisions kept for rollback
Default 10
Deep dive →
⑤ What runs in each Pod?groupthe Pod template
templateobjectrequireda full Pod spec plus labels

Changing it creates a new ControllerRevision and starts an update. The controller adds identity (name, hostname, subdomain, pod-index label) on top.

•metadata.labelsobjectrequiredmust match selector
•spec.initContainerslistinit-role: ordinal → primary or clone
•spec.containerslistrequiredpostgres with probes
•spec.topologySpreadConstraintslistone member per zone
•spec.terminationGracePeriodSecondsinttime to shut down cleanly; 60s for PostgreSQL
•spec.volumeslistConfigMap volumes; the PVC volume is added by the template name
Written by Kubernetesgroupdo not set these yourself
status.replicas / readyReplicas / availableReplicasintcounts
Deep dive →
status.currentRevision / updateRevisionstringold and new template hashes
Deep dive →
•status.updatedReplicasintPods already on updateRevision

3.1① Who am I? — names, labels and roles

Turning the ordinal into a role

Kubernetes gives each Pod an ordinal; it does not give it a role. The app decides. Here the init container reads the pod-index label through the downward API:

YAMLorders-db-stateful-set.yaml (init container env)
env:
  - name: POD_ORDINAL
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef:
        fieldPath: metadata.labels['apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index']
BASHinit-role.sh (from orders-db-config-map)
if [ "$POD_ORDINAL" = "0" ]; then exit 0; fi            # primary
if [ -s "$PGDATA/PG_VERSION" ]; then exit 0; fi        # replica, data already there
pg_basebackup -h orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service ...
Older pattern

Before the pod-index label (beta 1.28, GA 1.32), scripts parsed the hostname: ORD=${HOSTNAME##*-}. It still works and you will see it in older charts.

3.2② How many, and in what order?

In one sentenceOrderedReady starts members one by one and only after the previous one is Ready; Parallel starts them all at once.

replicas says how many; podManagementPolicy says how they come and go; minReadySeconds says how long a Pod must stay Ready before the controller trusts it.

Step 1 / 3OrderedReady: create one by one
OUTPUTkubectl get pods -wexample output
NAME                       READY   STATUS     AGE
orders-db-stateful-set-0   1/1     Running    95s
orders-db-stateful-set-1   1/1     Running    55s
orders-db-stateful-set-2   0/1     Init:0/1   5s
Step 2 / 3Parallel: all at once
Good for

Peers that do not depend on each other at start (Cassandra, a sharded cache), or faster recovery of large sets. Not for orders-db: the replicas would clone before the primary exists, then retry until it does.

Step 3 / 3⚖ Comparison
OrderedReadyParallel
Create0 → N-1, wait for Readyall at once
Scale downN-1 → 0, one by oneall chosen Pods at once
Updatesone at a time from the topone at a time from the top (same)
Broken pod-0blocks pods 1+others still start
Change later?no (immutable)no (immutable)

3.3⑤ The template — and what you may change later

In one sentenceOnly replicas, template, update settings, retention, ordinals and minReadySeconds can change; everything else is fixed at creation.

Every field in spec is either changeable (the controller reacts) or fixed at creation. Knowing which is which saves you from Forbidden: updates to statefulset spec for fields other than ….

FieldChange later?What happens
replicasyesPods added or removed in order; no new revision
templateyesnew ControllerRevision, rolling update (or wait for OnDelete)
updateStrategy, partitionyestakes effect on the next reconcile
minReadySeconds, revisionHistoryLimityesimmediately
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicyyesowner references on PVCs are updated
ordinals.startyesPods outside the new range are removed, new ones created
selectornorejected
serviceNamenorejected
volumeClaimTemplatesnorejected — see 5.4 to resize
podManagementPolicynorejected
OUTPUTkubectl apply after editing volumeClaimTemplatesexample output
The StatefulSet "orders-db-stateful-set" is invalid: spec: Forbidden: updates to statefulset spec for fields other than 'replicas', 'ordinals', 'template', 'updateStrategy', 'persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy' and 'minReadySeconds' are forbidden
✕ When it failsTo change an immutable field: kubectl delete sts orders-db-stateful-set --cascade=orphan, edit, kubectl apply. The orphaned Pods and PVCs are adopted by the new object because the selector matches.

3.4Written by Kubernetes

4

Headless Service & DNS

4.0How the headless Service works

In one sentenceThe headless Service turns each Pod's hostname and subdomain into a DNS record that points straight at the Pod IP.

The StatefulSet does not create DNS names; it only writes hostname and subdomain on each Pod. The headless Service whose name equals subdomain is what makes CoreDNS publish <hostname>.<subdomain>. Delete the Service and the names stop resolving; the Pods keep running.

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which Pods does it name?selectorthe guest list
② What makes it headless?clusterIP: None · publishNotReadyAddressesa phone book instead of a switchboard
③ Which ports?portsthe extension numbers
YAMLorders-db-headless-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Which Pods does it give names to?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  # ② What makes it headless?
  clusterIP: None# no virtual IP: DNS returns the Pod IPs themselves
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true# publish a Pod's DNS record before it is Ready (peer discovery)
  # ③ Which ports?
  ports:
    - name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
YAMLorders-db-read-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-read-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Which Pods receive reads?
  selector:
    app: orders-db# all members; only Ready Pods get traffic
  # ② How is it reached?
  type: ClusterIP# one stable virtual IP, load-balanced by kube-proxy
  # ③ Which ports?
  ports:
    - name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres

📌 RememberAfter pod-1 restarts, its record changes to the new IP within seconds; clients that cache DNS for long (JVM default, some drivers) may hold the old IP. Npgsql re-resolves on each new physical connection.

4.2publishNotReadyAddresses

In one sentenceTurn it on when members must find each other before they are Ready; give clients a separate Service that only lists Ready Pods.

DNS records exist as soon as a Pod has an IP, even before it is Ready. Peers can find each other while bootstrapping. Clients that resolve the headless name may get an IP that does not accept connections yet.

YAML
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true

Only Ready Pods appear. Safer for clients; but a member that must be reachable before it is Ready (Kafka KRaft, ZooKeeper, etcd forming quorum) never becomes reachable, and the cluster never forms.

YAML
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
truefalse
DNS before Readyyesno
Quorum systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka)neededdeadlock risk
Clients may hit a starting Podyes — use the read Service for clientsno
orders-db choice

true on the headless Service (for replication), and the normal orders-db-read-service (Ready Pods only) for application reads.

4.3Headless Service vs read Service

In one sentenceUse the headless Service to reach a specific member and the normal Service to spread reads.
orders-db-headless-serviceorders-db-read-service
clusterIPNonea VIP, 172.20.91.14
DNS answerPod IPs (one or all)the VIP
Who balancesthe clientkube-proxy (iptables/IPVS)
Reach one exact Podyes, by nameno
Not-ready Podslisted (publishNotReadyAddresses)never
Used byreplication, writes to pod-0order-service reads

4.4Request routing from order-service

In one sentenceWrites use the primary's stable DNS name, reads use a ClusterIP Service, and nothing promotes a replica for you.

order-service is an ASP.NET Core Deployment. It holds two Npgsql data sources, one per connection string from order-service-config-map.

YAMLorder-service-config-map.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: order-service-config-map
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-service
data:
  # ① Where do writes go? (always the primary, by stable DNS name)
  ConnectionStrings__OrdersWrite: "Host=orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service;Port=5432;Database=orders;Username=orders"
  # ② Where do reads go? (any Ready member, through the ClusterIP)
  ConnectionStrings__OrdersRead: "Host=orders-db-read-service;Port=5432;Database=orders;Username=orders;Load Balance Hosts=false"
  # ③ Optional: let Npgsql find the primary itself across all members
  ConnectionStrings__OrdersPrimaryAny: "Host=orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service,orders-db-stateful-set-1.orders-db-headless-service,orders-db-stateful-set-2.orders-db-headless-service;Target Session Attributes=primary;Database=orders;Username=orders"
TEXTProgram.cs (order-service)
builder.Services.AddNpgsqlDataSource(
    builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("OrdersWrite")!, serviceKey: "write");
builder.Services.AddNpgsqlDataSource(
    builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("OrdersRead")!, serviceKey: "read");
✕ When it failsIf pod-0 dies, writes fail until it is back (usually under a minute on the same node, several minutes if its node is lost and EBS must re-attach). A plain StatefulSet never promotes pod-1. If that is not acceptable, use an operator (see 1.4).
5

Storage

5.0How StatefulSet storage works

In one sentenceThe StorageClass makes the disk, the template makes one claim per ordinal, and two separate policies decide when claims and disks are deleted.

Three objects decide the life of orders-db data: the StorageClass (how a disk is made and what happens at the end), the volumeClaimTemplate (one claim per ordinal) and the retention policy (whether the controller ever deletes those claims).

Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① What disk?storageClassName · parameters · storagethe shop and the size
② Where and when?volumeBindingModebuilt in the Pod's zone, on demand
③ Whose is it?volumeClaimTemplates · PVC nameone locker per ordinal
④ When does it go away?persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy · reclaimPolicytwo separate switches
YAMLgp3-encrypted-storage-class.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3-encrypted-storage-class
# ① Who creates the disk?
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
# ② What kind of disk?
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
  fsType: ext4
# ③ When and where is it created?
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer# create the EBS volume in the zone the Pod lands in
# ④ What happens at the end?
reclaimPolicy: Retain# deleting a PVC keeps the EBS volume (database data!)
allowVolumeExpansion: true
YAMLorders-db-stateful-set.yaml (storage part)
volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: gp3-encrypted-storage-class
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 20Gi
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
  whenDeleted: Retain
  whenScaled: Retain

5.1Binding and the zone trap

In one sentenceEach member is tied to the zone of its first disk; plan node capacity per zone, not just in total.

An EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone. With WaitForFirstConsumer it is created where the Pod first lands, and the PV records that zone. From then on the Pod can only run in that zone.

OUTPUTkubectl get pv pvc-8b07d4c1-… -o yaml (excerpt Kubernetes wrote)example output
nodeAffinity:
  required:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - key: topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone
        operator: In
        values:
        - me-central-1b
OUTPUTkubectl describe pod orders-db-stateful-set-1example output
Warning  FailedScheduling  0/9 nodes are available: 3 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict, 6 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints.
Fix

Keep at least two nodes per zone in the node group (or a Karpenter NodePool that can add nodes in every zone), and use topologySpreadConstraints so members start in different zones.

5.2PVC lifecycle

In one sentencePVCs outlive Pods, scale-downs and the StatefulSet itself; the same ordinal always gets the same claim back.
BASH
kubectl delete pod orders-db-stateful-set-1 -n jahez-prod
✓ ResultSame name, same PVC; the replica resumes streaming from where it was.
BASH
kubectl scale sts orders-db-stateful-set --replicas=1 -n jahez-prod
kubectl scale sts orders-db-stateful-set --replicas=3 -n jahez-prod
✕ When it failsOld replica data may be too old to catch up (WAL already recycled on the primary). init-role.sh sees PG_VERSION and reuses it, so the replica fails with requested WAL segment … has already been removed. Delete that PVC before scaling up, or teach the script to re-clone.
BASH
kubectl delete sts orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pvc -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db
OUTPUTexample output
statefulset.apps "orders-db-stateful-set" deleted
NAME                            STATUS   CAPACITY
data-orders-db-stateful-set-0   Bound    20Gi
data-orders-db-stateful-set-1   Bound    20Gi
data-orders-db-stateful-set-2   Bound    20Gi
✓ ResultRe-applying the StatefulSet re-uses all three PVCs with their data.

5.3PVC retention policy

In one sentenceTwo switches decide whether PVCs die with the StatefulSet and with scale-downs; both default to Retain.
whenDeletedwhenScaledDelete the StatefulSetScale 3 → 2Use for
RetainRetainPVCs keptdata-…-2 keptorders-db prod (default)
RetainDeletePVCs keptdata-…-2 deletedprod, where scaled-out members should start fresh
DeleteRetainPVCs deleteddata-…-2 keptrare
DeleteDeletePVCs deleteddata-…-2 deleteddev / preview environments
YAMLdev overlay
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
  whenDeleted: Delete
  whenScaled: Delete
📌 RememberA deleted PVC deletes the EBS volume only if the StorageClass has reclaimPolicy: Delete. With gp3-encrypted-storage-class (Retain) the PV becomes Released and the EBS volume stays — and keeps costing money until you delete it.
Versions

Alpha 1.23, beta 1.27 (on by default), GA 1.32. Works only when deletion goes through the controller; deleting with --cascade=orphan keeps PVCs regardless.

5.4Resizing volumes

In one sentenceGrow each PVC, wait for the filesystem, then recreate the StatefulSet object with --cascade=orphan so the template matches.
Step 1 / 3Patch each PVC
  • The template is immutable, but each PVC can grow if the StorageClass allows expansion.
BASH
for i in 0 1 2; do
  kubectl patch pvc data-orders-db-stateful-set-$i -n jahez-prod --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'
done
OUTPUTexample output
persistentvolumeclaim/data-orders-db-stateful-set-0 patched
persistentvolumeclaim/data-orders-db-stateful-set-1 patched
persistentvolumeclaim/data-orders-db-stateful-set-2 patched
Step 2 / 3Wait for the filesystem resize
  • The EBS CSI driver grows the volume online, then kubelet grows ext4. No restart is needed with current drivers.
BASH
kubectl get pvc -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CAP:.status.capacity.storage
OUTPUTexample output
NAME                            CAP
data-orders-db-stateful-set-0   50Gi
data-orders-db-stateful-set-1   50Gi
data-orders-db-stateful-set-2   50Gi
Step 3 / 3Make the template match
  • Otherwise a future pod-3 gets 20Gi. Recreate the StatefulSet object without touching Pods.
BASH
kubectl delete sts orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod --cascade=orphan
# edit storage: 50Gi in orders-db-stateful-set.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/orders-db/orders-db-stateful-set.yaml
OUTPUTexample output
statefulset.apps "orders-db-stateful-set" deleted
statefulset.apps/orders-db-stateful-set created
✓ ResultThe new StatefulSet adopts the three running Pods; no restart, no data movement.
✕ When it failsShrinking is never allowed: spec.resources.requests.storage: Forbidden: field can not be less than previous value.

Operations — the lifecycle of orders-db

6.1Scale up and down

In one sentenceScaling adds Pods from the next ordinal up, one at a time, and removes them from the top down, always leaving their PVCs.
Step 1 / 3Scale up 3 → 5
Who does the workyou → API server → StatefulSet controller
  • Only spec.replicas changes; no new revision.
  • pod-3 is created only after pod-2 is Ready, then pod-4.
  • Each gets a new PVC; topology spread puts pod-3 in 1a and pod-4 in 1b.
BASH
kubectl scale sts orders-db-stateful-set --replicas=5 -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db -w

6.2RollingUpdate and maxUnavailable

In one sentenceRolling updates replace Pods from the highest ordinal down; partition, maxUnavailable and minReadySeconds tune how far and how fast.

2.4 traced a full rolling update. The knobs that change it:

KnobEffect on orders-dbWatch out
partition: Nonly ordinals ≥ N updatePods below N keep the old template, even if deleted
maxUnavailable: 2pod-2 and pod-1 replaced togetherbeta in 1.35; never let it reach the primary's quorum
minReadySeconds: 10each Pod must stay Ready 10s before the nextslows rollouts, catches flapping Pods
readinessProbedecides "Ready"without it, the next Pod goes as soon as the container starts
terminationGracePeriodSecondstime for PostgreSQL to stop cleanlytoo short = crash recovery on restart
YAMLorders-db-stateful-set.yaml (update part)
updateStrategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    partition: 0
    maxUnavailable: 1
minReadySeconds: 10

6.3Partition canary

In one sentenceSet the partition, change the template, check the one updated member, then lower the partition to release the rest.
Step 1 / 4Fence the update to pod-2
Who does the workyou
  • Set the partition first, so changing the image cannot touch pods 0 and 1.
BASH
kubectl patch sts orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":2}}}}'
💡 Command hint
change the StatefulSet spec→new revision if the template changed→rolling update from the highest ordinal
kubectlthe Kubernetes CLI; talks to the API server of the current context
patchchange part of the spec in place
stsshort name for statefulset
orders-db-stateful-setthe StatefulSet name
-nnamespace to act in
jahez-prodthe Jahez production namespace
--type=mergemerge patch: only the given fields change
-pthe JSON/merge patch to apply
{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":2}}}}the change, as JSON
OUTPUTexample output
statefulset.apps/orders-db-stateful-set patched
Step 2 / 4Change the image
Who does the workyou → controller
  • A new revision is created.
  • Only pod-2 (ordinal ≥ 2) is replaced.
BASH
kubectl set image sts/orders-db-stateful-set postgres=ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.6 init-role=ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.6 -n jahez-prod

6.4OnDelete

In one sentenceWith OnDelete the controller records the new template but applies it only to Pods you delete.
Step 1 / 3Switch to OnDelete
Who does the workyou
  • Template changes now wait for you; nothing is replaced automatically.
BASH
kubectl patch sts orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"type":"OnDelete","rollingUpdate":null}}}'

Who does the workcontroller (waits)

6.5Rollback with ControllerRevisions

In one sentenceUndo copies an old ControllerRevision's template back as a new revision and rolls it out like any other change.
BASH
kubectl rollout history sts/orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod
kubectl rollout history sts/orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod --revision=1
kubectl rollout undo sts/orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod --to-revision=1
OUTPUTexample output
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         <none>
2         <none>
…
statefulset.apps/orders-db-stateful-set rolled back
✕ When it failsRollback restores the template, not the data. After a PostgreSQL major upgrade (16 → 17) the data directory is already converted; rolling back the image makes PostgreSQL refuse to start. Test majors with a partition canary and a backup.

6.6A stuck rollout and the forced rollback

In one sentenceA broken new Pod freezes the rollout; repair it by restoring the template and deleting the broken Pod.

Who does the workyou

  • pod-2 is replaced and never becomes Ready.

kubectl set image sts/orders-db-stateful-set postgres=ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.6-bad -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db

Step 2 / 4The rollout stops — by design
Who does the workStatefulSet controller
  • pods 0 and 1 are protected: the controller waits for pod-2 to be Ready.
  • rollout status waits forever.

  • Undo restores the good template.

  • The controller recreates pod-2 from the current (good) template.

📌 RememberFixing a stuck StatefulSet always takes two actions: fix the template, then delete the Pods that already got the bad one.

6.7Delete

In one sentenceDeleting a StatefulSet removes its Pods but never its PVCs by default; force-deleting a Pod can create two members with one identity.
BASH
kubectl delete sts orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod
OUTPUTexample output
statefulset.apps "orders-db-stateful-set" deleted
  • Pods are deleted; with the default background cascade they go at the same time, not in reverse order.
  • PVCs, Services, Secret and ConfigMap stay.
  • For an ordered shutdown, scale to 0 first, then delete.
BASH
kubectl delete sts orders-db-stateful-set -n jahez-prod --cascade=orphan
  • The object goes; Pods keep running with no controller.
  • Used to change immutable fields: re-apply and the new object adopts them.
BASH
kubectl delete pod orders-db-stateful-set-1 -n jahez-prod
  • Recreated with the same name and PVC.
  • The safe way to restart one member.
BASH
kubectl delete pod orders-db-stateful-set-1 -n jahez-prod --force --grace-period=0
✕ When it failsThe API forgets the Pod immediately even if its node is only unreachable. The controller creates a new pod-1 while the old one may still run and write to the same disk — two members with one identity. Do this only when you know the node is really dead.

What ends or breaks a StatefulSet

What ends or breaks itPodsPVCsData
kubectl delete stsdeletedkept (Retain)safe
--cascade=orphankeep runningkeptsafe
namespace deleteddeleteddeletedEBS kept only with reclaimPolicy Retain
whenDeleted: Delete + delete stsdeleteddeleteddepends on reclaimPolicy
selector edited— (rejected)——
zone outagePending until zone returnskeptsafe, unreachable

The complete StatefulSet file is in 3.0.

6.8PodDisruptionBudget and node drains

In one sentenceThe PDB lets drains take at most one orders-db member at a time; other kinds of deletion ignore it.
YAMLorders-db-pdb.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: orders-db-pdb
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Which Pods does it protect?
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db
  # ② How many may be down by choice (drain, upgrade)?
  maxUnavailable: 1
BASH
kubectl get pdb orders-db-pdb -n jahez-prod
kubectl drain ip-10-40-45-7.me-central-1.compute.internal --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
OUTPUTexample output
NAME            MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
orders-db-pdb   N/A             1                 1                     9d

evicting pod jahez-prod/orders-db-stateful-set-1
pod/orders-db-stateful-set-1 evicted
OUTPUTsecond drain while pod-1 is still startingexample output
error when evicting pods/"orders-db-stateful-set-2" -n "jahez-prod" (will retry after 5s): Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.
📌 RememberThe PDB guards evictions (drains, Karpenter consolidation, EKS node upgrades). It does not guard rolling updates, scale-down or kubectl delete pod.

7.1Command cards

In one sentenceThirteen commands cover deploying, inspecting, scaling, updating, rolling back, deleting and debugging a StatefulSet.
kubectl apply
Create or update objects from files to match what is in git.
In one sentenceSends every manifest in the folder to the API server; the StatefulSet controller then does the rest.

Watch out

7.2Troubleshooting

In one sentenceFind the stage first — API, controller, scheduler, storage, node, readiness or DNS — and the fix follows.
#Symptom / messageCauseFix
1Forbidden: updates to statefulset spec for fields other than …immutable field changeddelete --cascade=orphan and re-apply (3.3)
1selector does not match template labelslabel typomake selector.matchLabels ⊆ template labels
2pod-1 never createdpod-0 not Ready (OrderedReady)fix pod-0 first: kubectl describe pod orders-db-stateful-set-0
2rollout stuck on pod-2bad templateundo + delete pod-2 (6.6)
3volume node affinity conflictno free node in the PV's zoneadd capacity in that zone (5.1)
4PVC Pending, waiting for first consumernormal until the Pod is scheduledlook at the Pod, not the PVC
4Multi-Attach errorold node still holds the EBS volumewait ~6 min for force-detach, or confirm the node is gone
5init-role loops waiting for orders-db-stateful-set-0…headless Service missing or wrong serviceNamecreate it; names must match
5requested WAL segment … has already been removedstale replica PVCdelete that PVC and let it re-clone
6Running but 0/1 Readyreadiness probe failingkubectl exec … -- pg_isready
7NXDOMAIN for orders-db-stateful-set-0Pod name alone is not a DNS nameuse <pod>.orders-db-headless-service

Practices & labs

CKAD-style tasks with hidden solutions, then the SRE habits and a one-page cheat sheet.

CKAD labs

8.1Six hands-on tasks

In one sentenceBuild, scale, canary, repair, parallelise and clean up a StatefulSet in the jahez-lab namespace.
Lab 1 · Create a StatefulSet with stable DNS
~8 min · namespace jahez-lab
Task

In jahez-lab, create a headless Service menu-cache-headless-service and a StatefulSet menu-cache-stateful-set running redis:7.4-alpine with 3 replicas, AOF on, a 1Gi PVC per Pod mounted at /data. Prove that menu-cache-stateful-set-1 resolves by name.

Show solution
BASH
kubectl create namespace jahez-lab
kubectl apply -f menu-cache-headless-service.yaml -f menu-cache-stateful-set.yaml
YAMLmenu-cache-headless-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-cache-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-lab
spec:

  ports:

YAMLmenu-cache-stateful-set.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: menu-cache-stateful-set
  namespace: jahez-lab
spec:
  # ① Who am I?
  serviceName: menu-cache-headless-service
  selector:

  template:

        - name: redis
          image: redis:7.4-alpine
          args: ["--appendonly", "yes"]
          ports:
            - name: redis

Lab 2 · Scale and prove PVCs survive
~5 min · namespace jahez-lab
Task

Write menu-a into menu-cache-stateful-set-2, scale to 1, scale back to 3, and show the key is still there.

Show solution
BASH
kubectl exec menu-cache-stateful-set-2 -n jahez-lab -- redis-cli set menu menu-a
kubectl scale sts menu-cache-stateful-set -n jahez-lab --replicas=1

"menu-a"

Show solution

~6 min · namespace jahez-lab
Task

~5 min · namespace jahez-lab
Task

Create search-node-stateful-set (image nginx:1.27, 4 replicas, headless Service search-node-headless-service) whose Pods all start at the same time.

9

SRE practices & cheat sheet

9.1SRE practices

In one sentenceTreat each member as a pet: spread it, protect it, probe it honestly, canary its changes and back it up outside Kubernetes.
Headless Service first, names must match

serviceName = Service name; put the Service in a file that sorts before the StatefulSet.

Connect by DNS, never by IP

Writes to orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service, reads to orders-db-read-service.

Real readiness probes

OrderedReady and rolling updates trust readiness. pg_isready, not "process is running".

Spread across zones, plan capacity per zone

topologySpreadConstraints on zone; keep spare nodes in each of 1a/1b/1c because PVs pin members to zones.

PDB maxUnavailable: 1

Protects against drains and Karpenter consolidation taking two members.

Canary every image change

partition = replicas-1, verify, then 0. Back up before PostgreSQL major upgrades; rollback does not undo data.

Back up outside the cluster

Nightly pg_dump or WAL-G to S3 from a CronJob, and EBS snapshots. A StatefulSet is not a backup.

Clean up PVCs and Released PVs

Retain everywhere means orphaned EBS volumes; review them monthly.

Alerts (kube-state-metrics + kubelet)

YAMLprometheus-rule (excerpt)
groups:
  - name: orders-db-statefulset
    rules:
      - alert: OrdersDbReplicasNotReady
        expr: kube_statefulset_status_replicas_ready{namespace="jahez-prod",statefulset="orders-db-stateful-set"} < kube_statefulset_replicas{namespace="jahez-prod",statefulset="orders-db-stateful-set"}
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: critical
      - alert: OrdersDbRolloutStuck
        expr: kube_statefulset_status_current_revision{namespace="jahez-prod"} unless kube_statefulset_status_update_revision{namespace="jahez-prod"}
        for: 30m
        labels:
          severity: warning
      - alert: OrdersDbVolumeFilling
        expr: kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes{namespace="jahez-prod",persistentvolumeclaim=~"data-orders-db-stateful-set-.*"} / kubelet_volume_stats_capacity_bytes < 0.15
        for: 15m
        labels:
          severity: warning

orders-db-config-map.yaml
ConfigMap · jahez-prod
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: orders-db-config-map
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
data:
  # ① What runs once, on the primary's very first start?
  10-replication.sh: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e
    psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d postgres <<-SQL
      CREATE ROLE ${REPLICATION_USER} WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD '${REPLICATION_PASSWORD}';
    SQL
    echo "host replication ${REPLICATION_USER} 0.0.0.0/0 scram-sha-256" >> "$PGDATA/pg_hba.conf"
  # ② How does each Pod decide its role?
  init-role.sh: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e
    # POD_ORDINAL comes from the apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index label
    if [ "$POD_ORDINAL" = "0" ]; then
      echo "ordinal 0 -> primary: the postgres entrypoint runs initdb itself"
      exit 0
    fi
    if [ -s "$PGDATA/PG_VERSION" ]; then
      echo "ordinal $POD_ORDINAL -> replica data already on the PVC, reuse it"
      exit 0
    fi
    PRIMARY=orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service
    until pg_isready -h "$PRIMARY" -p 5432; do echo "waiting for $PRIMARY"; sleep 2; done
    PGPASSWORD="$REPLICATION_PASSWORD" pg_basebackup -h "$PRIMARY" -U "$REPLICATION_USER" \
      -D "$PGDATA" -R -X stream -P
    echo "ordinal $POD_ORDINAL -> cloned from $PRIMARY, standby.signal written"
orders-db-headless-service.yaml
Service · jahez-prod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Which Pods does it give names to?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  # ② What makes it headless?
  clusterIP: None# no virtual IP: DNS returns the Pod IPs themselves
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true# publish a Pod's DNS record before it is Ready (peer discovery)
  # ③ Which ports?
  ports:
    - name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
